Superstitious
soo-per-STISH-us
adj. (excessively or irrationally devoted to religious observance, as charged by an unbelieving or dismissive observer)
From Latin superstitio, excessive fear of the gods or irrational religious belief, from superstare, to stand over or survive; the term has long been a weapon used by skeptics against sincere religious devotion of any kind.

Biblical Definition

Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious.

Paul opens his sermon at the Areopagus with an observation about Athenian religiosity that is double-edged: the word translated superstitious can describe either commendable reverence or excessive, misdirected religious devotion, and Paul's own sermon makes clear he means the latter — a city so crowded with idols that it had erected an altar to an unknown god, covering every religious base without actually knowing the true God behind any of them. Paul does not mock religious seriousness itself; he redirects it, declaring unto them the God whom they ignorantly worship, the Creator who made the world and all things therein, who now commands all men everywhere to repent in light of the resurrection and coming judgment. The Athenians prided themselves on philosophical sophistication while Paul's own gospel would later be dismissed by exactly that sophistication as foolishness. The scene stands as a permanent pattern: cultured unbelief frequently charges biblical religion with the irrationality it cannot see in its own idols, intellectual or otherwise, and the only answer is Paul's own — proclaim the true God plainly rather than conceding the charge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from SUPERSTITION: excessive reverence, or false, unfounded religious fear and observance; superstitious: addicted to or marked by such excess.

expand to see more

SUPERSTITION, n. Excessive exactness or rigor in religious opinions or practice; extreme and unfounded religious fear.

SUPERSTITIOUS, a. Addicted to superstition; full of idle fancies in religion.

Acts 17:22 records Paul's double-edged opening charge against Athenian religiosity before the Areopagus.

Paul redirects, rather than dismisses, the Athenians' religious seriousness toward the true God.

The altar to the unknown god exemplifies devotion without true knowledge of its object.

Key Scripture

Act 17:22 — "Then Paul stood in the midst of Mars' hill, and said, Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are too superstitious."

Modern Corruption

Modern scientific materialism and New Atheism apply superstitious indiscriminately to all revealed religion, including biblical faith in the true and living God, collapsing Paul's distinction between idolatrous devotion and genuine knowledge of the Creator.

expand to see more

Writers in the New Atheist tradition, and the broader scientism of much secular academia, use superstitious as a catch-all dismissal of any claim to divine revelation, treating biblical faith as indistinguishable from the Athenian altars Paul actually confronted.

Paul's own sermon refuses that collapse: Athens was superstitious precisely because it worshiped an unknown god, many gods covering every contingency without true knowledge of any; the gospel is the opposite move, declaring the one true God who made the world, commands repentance, and has fixed a day of judgment by a risen Christ. Biblical faith is not superstition answered by enlightenment; it is the true knowledge Athens's superstition was groping after without finding.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin superstitio, excessive religious fear, superstitious has long served as a weapon against sincere devotion; Acts 17:22 shows Paul redirecting rather than conceding the charge.

Superstitio, Latin for excessive religious fear, underlies superstitious.

The term has served unbelieving sophistication as a weapon against devotion of any kind.

Acts 17:22 records Paul's charge against Athenian religiosity at the Areopagus.

Paul redirects the Athenians' devotion to the true God rather than mocking devotion itself.

Modern scientism reapplies the charge to biblical faith, collapsing Paul's own distinction.
